subChunks.title: Passenger Lists, Naturalisations & the Immigrant's Paper Trail
subChunks.hookHtml: Every ancestor who crossed an ocean or a border left a paper trail — in the country they left and the country they arrived in. Immigration and emigration records span departure manifests, ship logs, port registers, border crossing cards, naturalisation papers, and a dozen derivative records. The key insight for genealogists is that the information available about an immigrant changes dramatically depending on the year of arrival: a passenger arriving at New York in 1855 left almost no information; one arriving in 1910 filled out a 30-column manifest that might tell you their last place of residence, their physical description, their intended US contact, and a named relative in the old country. Understanding what each era's records contain is essential for extracting maximum value.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
US passenger lists — by era

US passenger records fall into three broad periods with very different information content:

  • Pre-1820: almost no formal passenger records exist for arrivals. Occasional ship logs, port authority lists, and newspaper notices of arrivals survive but are fragmentary. For colonial-era immigrants, look to church records, land records, and naturalisation records.
  • 1820–1891 (Customs passenger lists): the Passenger Act 1819 required ship captains to file passenger manifests with US Customs. These customs lists give name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. They do not give a specific town of origin before the 1890s — 'Germany' or 'Ireland' is typical. Indexed and digitised on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Fold3.
  • 1892–1957 (Immigration passenger lists): from 1892, the new federal immigration bureaucracy took over, and the manifests became progressively more detailed. The key transition is 1906, when new legislation required manifests to record:
    • Last place of residence in the old country (specific town, not just country)
    • Contact person in the old country (name and relationship — usually a parent, sibling, or spouse)
    • Contact person in the US (name, address, and relationship)
    • Physical description (height, weight, hair colour, eye colour, distinguishing marks)
    • Amount of money carried
    • Whether destined for a job already arranged
    Post-1906 manifests are therefore the most genealogically rich passenger records for the mass immigration era. Available on Ancestry, Ellis Island Foundation (ellisisland.org, free), and FamilySearch.

Ellis Island and other ports

Ellis Island processed approximately 12 million immigrants between 1892 and 1954 — but it was not the only US port of entry. Other major ports include Baltimore (Castle Garden, 1855–1890, then the Baltimore Immigration Station), Boston, New Orleans, Philadelphia, and Galveston. Immigrants from Mexico and Canada crossed land borders, recorded in separate registers. Key points:

  • The Ellis Island database (ellisisland.org) is a major genealogical resource but covers only New York arrivals at Ellis Island. Arrivals at Baltimore, Boston, Philadelphia, New Orleans, and Galveston are in separate records on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
  • Castle Garden (lower Manhattan) pre-dated Ellis Island as New York's immigrant reception centre, 1855–1890. Records are at the New York State Archives.
  • Canadian border crossings by immigrants who first arrived in Canada are recorded in NARA border crossing cards (Series M1462 and M1478) — these can provide details for ancestors who came via Canada before proceeding to the US.

British departure records

For British and Irish emigrants, departure records complement arrival records:

  • Board of Trade outward passenger lists (BT27 at TNA): from 1890, every ship departing a British port filed an outward passenger list. These give name, age, occupation, and intended destination country. They are on Ancestry and FindMyPast. For emigrants before 1890, the Hamburg Emigration Lists (for Germans transiting through Hamburg) and various passenger list projects are the primary departure records.
  • Emigrant information from UK census: the UK census asked birthplace but not emigration. However, ships' passengers lists from British ports can be combined with the UK census (an ancestor present in the census year but absent in the next) to establish emigration dates.

Naturalisation records — the most detailed immigration documents

Naturalisation records are often the most genealogically valuable immigration documents because they were created long after arrival and required substantial personal information:

  • Declaration of Intention ('first papers'): filed up to seven years before naturalisation, renouncing allegiance to the country of birth. Post-1906, these give: name, age, birthplace (specific town), physical description, date and port of arrival, name of ship.
  • Petition for Naturalisation ('second papers'): the formal application, giving name, address, occupation, wife's name, wife's birthplace, children's names and ages, date of arrival, and more.
  • Before 1906: naturalisations could take place in any court (federal, state, or local). Records are scattered across court archives at the state and county level. NARA holds many federal court naturalisations; state archives hold state court ones.
  • After 1906: all naturalisations were handled by the federal Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS). Records are at NARA. The post-1906 petition is the most detailed document in the US immigration record landscape.
  • Women and naturalisation: before 1922, a woman's citizenship followed her husband's (coverture). She became a US citizen automatically when her husband naturalised — but was denaturalised if she married a non-citizen. The Cable Act 1922 changed this. Women who naturalised independently before 1922 filed their own papers; those who derived citizenship through a husband appear in his petition only.

Other immigration-era records

  • Immigrant inspection cards and medical records: at Ellis Island, immigrants were examined for disease and disability. Detention records and medical examination cards survive in NARA holdings for selected individuals.
  • HIAS (Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society): assisted Jewish immigrants; case files can give specific old-country details.
  • Steamship company records: companies such as Cunard, White Star, and Hamburg-Amerika maintained their own passenger records. Some survive in company archives or have been published.
  • Canadian immigration records: Library and Archives Canada holds passenger manifests at Library and Archives Canada (collectionscanada.gc.ca), with the Border Entry index on FamilySearch.

storyBeats.text: Theodora unrolls a long, narrow document — a post-1906 ship manifest, thirty columns wide, each row a passenger. She runs her finger along one row, reading aloud.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Compare a passenger arriving at New York in 1880 with one arriving in 1910. The 1880 manifest: name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin. That is it. You know they arrived. You do not know where in Ireland or Germany or Poland they came from. Now look at the 1910 manifest. Thirty columns. Name. Last place of residence — specific village, not just country. Destination in the US. Contact person in the old country: name, relationship, town. Contact person in the US: name, address, relationship. Physical description. Amount of money. Whether they have been to the US before. Whether they are meeting a relative. Thirty columns of information, required by law.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The contact person in the old country is everything. A man sailing from Hamburg in 1910 names his mother, still in the village. Her name. The village name. The county. You have bridged the Atlantic in a single field. Then you go to JRI-Poland or the parish records of that village with the mother's name and you find the family. That is why the 1906 immigration act matters so much to genealogists: it was not designed for us, but it gave us everything.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And then the naturalisation papers. After 1906, the Declaration of Intention — 'first papers' — gives birthplace as a specific town. The Petition for Naturalisation gives wife's name, birthplace, and country; children's names and ages. A father naturalised in 1912 with three children listed in his petition — three names, three ages, a family unit. Check the petition against the census and the passenger list and you have a constellation of evidence. The immigrant's paper trail is dense if you know where to look.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor immigration records

Retrieve from memory:

  • What was the key change in US passenger manifests after 1906, and why does it matter for genealogists?
  • What is the difference between a Declaration of Intention and a Petition for Naturalisation?
  • What are the BT27 records at TNA and what do they cover?
  • Why were women's naturalisations treated differently from men's before 1922?
  • Besides Ellis Island, name two other major US ports of immigration entry.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
After 1906, US passenger manifests were required to record the immigrant's last specific place of residence in the old country, a contact person (name, relationship, town) in the old country, and a contact person (name, address, relationship) in the US. This transforms the manifest from a bare arrival record into a bridge document that can give a specific European village of origin — the most direct route to the old-country record landscape.

The Declaration of Intention ('first papers') was an initial renunciation of foreign allegiance, filed up to seven years before naturalisation, giving name, age, specific birthplace, physical description, and arrival details. The Petition for Naturalisation ('second papers') was the formal naturalisation application, giving name, address, wife's name and birthplace, children's names and ages — the more genealogically detailed document. Both are at NARA for federal court naturalisations after 1906.

BT27 records at TNA are Board of Trade outward passenger lists from 1890, covering ships departing British ports — available on Ancestry and FindMyPast. They complement arrival records by confirming departure details and destination.

Before the Cable Act 1922, a woman's citizenship derived from her husband's under coverture principles: she became a US citizen when her husband naturalised and was denaturalised if she married a non-citizen. She had no independent naturalisation status. Post-1922, women could naturalise independently.

Other major US ports include Baltimore, Boston, Philadelphia, New Orleans, and Galveston. Records for each are in separate collections on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Maximising the value of immigration records

You find the following 1908 US passenger manifest entry:

Name: Stanislaw Kowalski. Age: 24. Occupation: labourer. Last residence: Kielce, Russia. Contact in old country: Jan Kowalski (father), Kielce, Russia. Contact in US: brother Józef Kowalski, 47 Elm Street, Chicago, Illinois. Amount: $12. Previously in US: no. Married: no. Destination: Illinois.

Extract every genealogical lead this entry provides and explain what further records you would search for each lead.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Genealogical leads:

1. Stanislaw Kowalski: born c.1884 (aged 24 in 1908), unmarried labourer from Kielce. Search: 1910 US census for Stanislaw Kowalski, Illinois (specifically Chicago area). Search: US naturalisation records (Declaration of Intention filed within years of 1908 arrival, then Petition).

2. Kielce, Russia: Kielce was in the Russian-controlled Kingdom of Poland. This identifies the archive and record type: metrical books at the Kielce state archive or indexed on JRI-Poland and Szukajwarchiwach.pl. Search: birth register for Stanislaw Kowalski in Kielce c.1884, which should name both parents.

3. Jan Kowalski (father) in Kielce: a named relative still in the old country with a specific address. Search: Kielce vital records for Jan Kowalski's own birth (c.1850–1860) and his marriage to Stanislaw's mother. The mother's name will appear in Stanislaw's birth register.

4. Józef Kowalski (brother) at 47 Elm Street, Chicago: Stanislaw's brother is in Chicago. Search: 1900 and 1910 US census for Józef Kowalski at or near that address. Józef's census entry will give his birth year, birthplace, and immigration year — potentially earlier than Stanislaw. His naturalisation papers should also give their father's name and Kielce as birthplace.

5. Name variant search: 'Stanislaw' may appear as 'Stanley' in US records. 'Kowalski' may be misspelled in census indexes. Search with variant names when the primary search fails.

6. Amount ($12): notes economic circumstance but no additional genealogical leads.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why the year an ancestor arrived in America matters so much for what information you can find about them — and what the difference is between a pre-1906 and post-1906 passenger manifest.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The first step in US naturalisation ('first papers') — a formal renunciation of foreign allegiance giving the applicant's name, birthplace (specific town after 1906), physical description, and arrival details; filed up to seven years before the petition.

The formal naturalisation application ('second papers') giving name, address, occupation, wife's name and birthplace, children's names and ages, and arrival details — the most genealogically detailed document in the US immigration record landscape.
TNA series of Board of Trade outward passenger lists (1890 onward) for ships departing British ports, giving name, age, occupation, and intended destination — available on Ancestry and FindMyPast.
New York's immigrant reception centre before Ellis Island (1855–1890), located at the tip of Manhattan; records are at the New York State Archives and online via the Castle Garden database.

US legislation that ended the automatic derivative citizenship of wives through their husbands' naturalisation, allowing women to naturalise independently — changing how pre- and post-1922 women's citizenship records must be searched.

questions.questionHtml: What key genealogical information did post-1906 US passenger manifests include that earlier manifests did not?
options: The immigrant's last specific place of residence in the old country, a named contact person in the old country (with relationship and address), and a named contact person in the US — enabling direct identification of the European town of origin
The immigrant's religion, language spoken, and intended occupation in the US
The name of the ship's captain and the vessel's tonnage
The immigrant's previous criminal record and health status
questions.correctAnswer: The immigrant's last specific place of residence in the old country, a named contact person in the old country (with relationship and address), and a named contact person in the US — enabling direct identification of the European town of origin
questions.explanationHtml: The 1906 US immigration legislation required manifests to collect much more detailed information than earlier customs lists. The most genealogically valuable additions were: (1) last place of residence in the old country — a specific village, not just a country; (2) contact person in the old country — name, relationship, and town (often a parent or sibling); (3) contact person in the US — name, address, and relationship. These three fields transformed the manifest into a bridge document between the New World arrival record and the Old World vital records. Pre-1906 manifests typically give only country of origin, age, sex, and occupation.

questions.questionHtml: You find an ancestor named Maria Kovač who arrived at New York in 1895, listed as coming from 'Austria.' The manifest gives no specific town. What is your next step to identify her specific European origin?
options: Search for her naturalisation petition — a post-1906 Declaration of Intention or Petition for Naturalisation would give her specific birthplace if she naturalised after 1906, even though she arrived before
Accept 'Austria' as sufficient and search Austrian national records broadly
The 1895 manifest is the most detailed record available; no further precision is possible from immigration records
Search the 1890 US census for her family — it will give her specific Austrian town
questions.correctAnswer: Search for her naturalisation petition — a post-1906 Declaration of Intention or Petition for Naturalisation would give her specific birthplace if she naturalised after 1906, even though she arrived before
questions.explanationHtml: Even though Maria arrived in 1895 with a bare 'Austria' country listing, she may have naturalised (or derived citizenship through a husband's naturalisation) after 1906. Post-1906 naturalisation documents require the applicant's specific birthplace — town, region, and country — which would give the precise detail missing from the 1895 manifest. Additionally, the Declaration of Intention gives physical description and arrival details that can corroborate her identity. If naturalisation records are unavailable (e.g., she naturalised via a pre-1906 husband), the 1900 and 1910 US census entries for Maria (giving immigration year and birthplace) combined with the US city directory for contact information might help narrow the search.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds a woman, Anna Müller, absent from US naturalisation records. They conclude she was never naturalised. Their colleague suggests Anna's citizenship may have derived from her husband's without any separate record. Who is correct and why?
options: The colleague is correct — before the Cable Act 1922, wives automatically became US citizens when their husbands naturalised; Anna may have derived citizenship through her husband's naturalisation file without filing any papers of her own
The original researcher is correct — every naturalised American citizen, male or female, filed their own papers
Both are wrong — women were not permitted to naturalise before 1922 under any circumstances
The colleague is correct, but only if Anna was born in a country that permitted dual citizenship
questions.correctAnswer: The colleague is correct — before the Cable Act 1922, wives automatically became US citizens when their husbands naturalised; Anna may have derived citizenship through her husband's naturalisation file without filing any papers of her own
questions.explanationHtml: Under US law before the Cable Act 1922, a woman's citizenship was derived from her husband's — a principle rooted in coverture. When her husband filed a Petition for Naturalisation and was naturalised, his wife automatically became a US citizen. The husband's petition often named the wife and children, and that document is the relevant record for Anna's citizenship. Anna would have filed her own papers only if she was unmarried or widowed at the time of naturalisation, or if she naturalised after 1922 under the Cable Act's new independent-citizenship regime. The absence of a separate naturalisation record for Anna before 1922 is expected, not anomalous — the researcher should search for her husband's naturalisation file instead.
